strengths: The problem is practically relevant. Combining adversarial generation of synthetic distributions with supervised dual-potential prediction is a potentially useful extension of learned Sinkhorn initialization, particularly when representative training data are unavailable.

Tables 1–2 report consistent improvements across four datasets: approximately 16% fewer iterations on average at marginal error 1e-3 and 33% fewer at 1e-2. Reporting marginal feasibility, transport-cost error, and wall-clock time provides useful evidence beyond prediction accuracy alone.

The presentation explains the mathematical setup and implementation clearly, including architectures, pseudocode, training hyperparameters, training cost, and a code link. Proposition 7 has a sound proof for its stated objective-gap bound. Retaining Sinkhorn refinement makes approximate predictions practically usable.
weaknesses: The central adversarial-training contribution is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison against a frozen generator, ordinary random synthetic distributions, or another non-adversarial sampling strategy with matched supervision and compute. Consequently, the experiments establish benefits from the complete learned initializer but do not establish why adversarial generation is necessary or beneficial.

Downstream convergence is compared only against all-ones initialization, despite discussing the initializers of Thornton and Cuturi and the learned approach of Amos et al. Figure 3 compares training losses using potential MSE, which directly favors the supervised objective, without comparing the resulting Sinkhorn convergence. Matched downstream comparisons are needed to establish the contribution relative to existing methods.

The universality claim exceeds the evidence. All experiments use smoothed 784-bin images, one fixed squared-Euclidean cost, and epsilon = 0.00025. This supports transfer across the tested image families, while performance on arbitrary fixed-dimension marginals remains unestablished. Tests with concentrated or highly imbalanced distributions and an epsilon sweep would directly address the stated motivation.

Section 3.3 overinterprets Proposition 7: a vanishing objective gap does not establish closeness of unregularized and regularized potentials or faster convergence after exponentiation. Unregularized potentials can remain nonunique even after centering. Moreover, the bound mn*epsilon is approximately 153.7 in the experiments, although ground costs are at most 2. The result therefore supplies little quantitative justification for the initialization in the evaluated regime.

The standalone barycenter claim is preliminary. Figure 7 provides four qualitative examples without reference barycenters, objective errors, or runtime comparisons. The assumed zero-mean prediction error is unverified, and unbiased objective values at fixed inputs would not by themselves establish accurate minimizers.

Reproducibility and practical efficiency need fuller documentation. Test-pair counts, independent training runs, confidence-interval construction, exact test smoothing, and timing batch sizes are unspecified. Numerical precision and stabilization also matter at the small epsilon used. Separately reporting initialization overhead and when inference savings recover the reported three-hour training cost would make the computational benefit easier to assess.
